explain.say: A real wall is not one material: plaster, brick, insulation, cladding, with air films on both faces. How do you add them up? Engineers borrowed a trick from electricity. Look at the wall: four layers, each resisting the heat a different amount. One square metre, 20 degrees inside and 0 outside.

explain.say: Each layer has a thermal resistance. For conduction it is L over k A; for a surface air film it is 1 over h A. Heat flow is like current, temperature difference like voltage, so Q equals delta T over R, just like Ohm's law. See the circuit: four resistors in series.

explain.say: Series resistances simply add: 0.10 plus 0.14 plus 1.25 plus 0.04 gives 1.53 kelvin per watt. So Q is 20 over 1.53, about 13 watts per square metre. Look at the resistor values: which layer does most of the work?

explain.say: The insulation, with 1.25 of the 1.53! The temperature drop across each layer is Q times its R, so the biggest drop happens across the biggest resistance. See the graph: the line falls gently through the brick, then plunges across the insulation from about 17 degrees to half a degree.

explain.say: Lovely. Without the insulation, Q would be 20 over 0.28, about 71 watts per square metre, more than five times worse! Real link: building codes give the U-value, which is 1 over the total R per square metre. Exam tip: layers side by side, like a window in a wall, are parallel resistances.

faq.q: Why does insulation matter so much in a wall?
faq.a: Insulation has a very low conductivity, so even a thin layer has a large thermal resistance. In series, that big resistance dominates the total and cuts the heat flow.

faq.q: Why is heat flow like electric current?
faq.a: Heat flow Q equals temperature difference over thermal resistance, just as current equals voltage over resistance. So series and parallel rules from circuits work for heat too.

faq.q: How do I find the temperature between layers?
faq.a: Find Q first, then subtract Q times each resistance in turn from the hot side temperature. The biggest resistance has the biggest temperature drop.

faq.q: What is the resistance of an air film?
faq.a: A surface where heat passes to or from air by convection has a resistance of 1 over h A. Still indoor air with h about 10 gives 0.1 kelvin per watt for one square metre.
The U-value is the overall heat transfer coefficient, one over the total resistance per square metre, in watts per square metre kelvin. Lower U means a better insulated wall.

facts: Thermal resistances in series add, just like electrical resistors.
The U-value of a wall is the reciprocal of its total thermal resistance per square metre.

quiz.say: Three layers in series have resistances of 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3 kelvin per watt. The temperature difference across them is 30 kelvin. What is the heat flow?
quiz.show: R = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3 K/W in series, ΔT = 30 K. Heat flow?

wrong.1: That divides by 3 as if taking an average resistance; series resistances add.
wrong.2: That multiplies the resistances in a parallel-like way; series ones just add to 1.0.

quiz.say: Across which layer of a composite wall is the temperature drop largest?
quiz.show: Where is the biggest temperature drop in a composite wall?

options.show: Across the layer with the largest thermal resistance
options.say: Across the layer with the largest thermal resistance

quiz.why: The same Q passes through every layer, so ΔT = Q × R is largest where R is largest.

wrong.1: A thick layer of a good conductor can still have a small resistance.
wrong.2: The outside film usually has a small resistance because wind makes h large.
